match.reason: None of the bank points teaches inverse circular functions: the Pythagorean identity, integrals and derivatives of trig functions are related to sine, cosine and tangent but do not define arcsin, arccos or arctan, their restricted domains or their graphs.

draft.title: Inverse circular functions
card: Sin, cos and tan repeat, so they are not one-to-one over all x. To have an inverse, each is restricted to a domain where it is one-to-one.
arcsin
the inverse of sin x on [−π/2, π/2]. It has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2].
arccos
the inverse of cos x on [0, π]. It has domain [−1, 1] and range [0, π].
arctan
the inverse of tan x on (−π/2, π/2). It has domain all real numbers and range (−π/2, π/2). Example: arcsin(1/2) = π/6, because sin(π/6) = 1/2.
draft.remember: An inverse swaps domain and range, and its answer lies in the restricted range.

a.q: What is the exact value of arccos(0)?
a.why: arccos(0) is the angle in [0, π] with cosine 0, which is π/2. The value 3π/2 also has cosine 0, but it lies outside the range [0, π].
a.clue: The answer must lie between 0 and π.

b.q: Which is the exact value of arcsin(−1/2)?
b.why: The answer must lie in [−π/2, π/2], and sin(−π/6) = −1/2. The value 11π/6 also has sine −1/2, but it is outside the range of arcsin. The positive π/6 gives sine +1/2.
b.clue: Check which angles fall inside the range of arcsin.

problems.detail: The worked example arcsin(1/2) = π/6 is attached to the end of the arctan bullet, so it reads as if it illustrates arctan. It belongs with the arcsin bullet or on its own line.

final.title: Inverse circular functions
card: Sin, cos and tan repeat, so each is restricted to a domain where it is one-to-one before it can have an inverse. The inverse swaps domain and range, and its graph is the reflection of the restricted graph in \(y = x\).
arcsin

the inverse of \(\sin x\) on \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), so it has domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\). For example, \(\arcsin\left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = \frac{\pi}{6}\), because \(\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\).
arccos
the inverse of \(\cos x\) on \([0, \pi]\). It has domain \([-1, 1]\) and range \([0, \pi]\).
arctan
the inverse of \(\tan x\) on \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). It has domain all real numbers and range \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

4.alt: The graph of \(y = \arctan x\) for all real \(x\). It rises through the origin and levels off towards the dashed horizontal asymptotes \(y = \frac{\pi}{2}\) and \(y = -\frac{\pi}{2}\), which it never reaches.

final.remember: Many angles share a sine, cosine or tangent. The inverse gives the one in its restricted range.

a.q: What is the exact value of \(\arccos(0)\)?
a.why: \(\arccos(0)\) is the angle in \([0, \pi]\) with cosine 0, which is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). The value \(\frac{3\pi}{2}\) also has cosine 0, but it lies outside the range \([0, \pi]\).
a.clue: The answer must lie between 0 and \(\pi\).

b.q: Which is the exact value of \(\arcsin\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)\)?
b.why: The answer must lie in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), and \(\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right) = -\frac{1}{2}\). The value \(\frac{11\pi}{6}\) also has sine \(-\frac{1}{2}\), but it is outside the range of arcsin. The positive \(\frac{\pi}{6}\) gives sine \(+\frac{1}{2}\).
b.clue: Check which angles fall inside the range of arcsin.
